title: A Real T. rex Named Gus Could Be Yours — If You Have $30 Million!
summary: Imagine digging in your backyard and finding a real dinosaur bone! That’s kind of what happened on a ranch in South Dakota. A man named Gary “Gus” Licking kept spotting T. rex teeth and fossil bits on his 6,500-acre property. He knew something big was underground. He was right! In 2021, a team dug up a nearly complete Tyrannosaurus rex skeleton. They named it “Gus” after him. Now, you can buy it — if you have $30 million. That’s enough to buy about 600,000 video game consoles! Gus is 38 feet long (longer than a school bus) and 12.5 feet tall (as tall as a one-story house). It lived about 67 million years ago, during the late Cretaceous period. The bones are going up for auction at Sotheby’s in New York City on Tuesday. The starting bid is $19 million. That’s a lot of allowance money! Dinosaur auctions are rare but not new. The first one was in 1997 for a T. rex named Sue, which sold for $8.4 million. In 2024, a stegosaurus called Apex sold for $44.6 million — the most ever. Some scientists worry that selling fossils to rich people means they might not be studied or shared with the public. Paleontologist Scott Persons says that kind of money could pay for years of research and new discoveries. Still, it’s pretty amazing that you can own a piece of history — if your piggy bank is big enough!
why_it_matters: Even if you can't buy a dinosaur, you can still visit fossils in museums, and maybe one day you'll become a paleontologist who discovers a brandnew species!

background_read: Many dinosaur fossils have been found in the badlands of South Dakota and Montana, places with dry, open land where ancient bones are slowly uncovered by wind and rain.
One of the most famous T. rex skeletons, Sue, sold for $8.4 million in 1997 and is now displayed in a museum for everyone to study and enjoy.
When rare fossils go to private buyers, paleontologists worry they may end up in someone's private collection instead of a museum where scientists and the public can learn from them.
Article_Structure: WHO: A rancher named Gary 'Gus' Licking and a team of fossil hunters
WHAT: Dug up a nearly complete Tyrannosaurus rex skeleton called Gus and are now selling it at auction
WHERE: Discovered on Licking's 6,500-acre ranch in South Dakota; the auction takes place at Sotheby's in New York City
WHY: To give someone the rare chance to own a real dinosaur skeleton, but also raising questions about whether such important fossils should be sold privately

perspectives.description: Some people see owning a dinosaur skeleton as a once-in-a-lifetime thrill, and sellers argue that high prices show how much we value natural history.
Paleontologists worry that when fossils are sold to private buyers, those bones might be locked away and never studied, which means we could lose chances to learn about how dinosaurs lived.
Big dinosaur auctions create worldwide interest and sometimes lead to fossils being loaned to museums later—but the high prices also make it almost impossible for museums to buy them.
